source.title: Foundation Models of Scientific Knowledge for Chemistry: Opportunities, Challenges and Lessons Learned
source.authors: Sameera Horawalavithana; Ellyn Ayton; Shivam Sharma; Scott Howland; Megha Subramanian; Scott Vasquez; Robin Cosbey; M. Glenski; Svitlana Volkova

record.tranche_reason: The study varies model size and measures validation cross-entropy loss on chemistry-focused language models, addressing the scaling question in a different domain. It does not fit scaling exponents or test extrapolation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports downstream benchmark results for many models and datasets, but the scaling discussion explicitly summarizes size trends for SciQ, HT-CC, ARC-E, and other benchmarks; the XL (4x) comparison also reports selected outcomes. It does not report a numerical validation-loss table or fitted power laws. No results test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, architecture-shape effects, other modalities, or fitting-choice sensitivity.
record.test_reason: The study trains GPT-NeoX models from scratch (0.18B–1.47B) on chemistry literature. It reports validation cross-entropy against model size (Figure 2) and zero-shot downstream results against size, explicitly revisiting Kaplan et al. This is a new setting (domain-specific scientific text). It fits no power law, exponent or extrapolation, and varies model size across less than one order of magnitude.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly wrong. The authors say validation loss falls with model size, 'confirming' Kaplan et al. They also say zero-shot performance rises with size on SciQ, HT-CC and ARC-E but shows no clear relationship elsewhere. Even so, they conclude that model size 'significantly contributes' to task performance, while pretraining loss may not be an ideal indicator of downstream results. They attribute the XL (4x) gains to more tokens and larger batch size.
record.recipe_differences: Uses autoregressive chemistry models and validation cross-entropy across four model sizes, but does not fit scaling laws or report exponents; the XL (4x) comparison changes batch size rather than isolating an optimal compute allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream outcomes differ by benchmark: the paper reports size-related gains for SciQ, HT-CC, and ARC-E but no clear size relationship on the remaining benchmarks. The XL (4x) model also differs from XL in batch size.
record.problems: The validation-loss result is presented in a figure without numerical values in the text, and the paper reports no fitted law or exponent. The tested model-size range is 0.18B–1.47B parameters. The downstream scale results are mixed across benchmarks, and no uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 4–5 report many additional model-by-dataset downstream scores. They are not separately extracted here because the paper's scaling discussion summarizes most of these results as task-level trends, while the XL (4x) comparison is recorded for the specific outcomes discussed in the text.

untested.parts: Power-law functional form, scaling with dataset size or compute, and range over several orders of magnitude (the sweep is under 10x in parameters).
All of it: no fitted law is used to predict larger runs.
All of it: there is no fixed-compute allocation search.
All of it: depth and width vary only together with parameter count.
All of it: the study uses text pretraining only, on a different text domain.
Predictability from pretraining loss: the authors speculate but do not relate loss to downstream scores.
All of it: no fits or fitting choices are compared.

missing.what: Pile-PubMed-Abstracts perplexity by size for each corpus. Several sweeps plateau or worsen at XL (AMiner 24.18→25.52, MAG 24.78→26.09, S2ORC 42.14→42.35).
Lambada and WikiText perplexity by size for each corpus. Most fall with size, but not monotonically (e.g. AMiner L 661.81 vs XL 786.22).
XL (4x) vs XL Pile perplexity (23.01 vs 31.03), from a 4x token increase.
The S model outperforms XL on 21% of in-domain and 34% of out-of-domain tasks.

record.verdict_notes: The tranche is set to T3 (chemistry-domain setting) rather than T2. Individual-corpus models saw about 10B tokens and combined models about 20B, the same for every size. Larger models are therefore likely data-limited, which is relevant to V1's 'other two not the bottleneck' condition. No uncertainty estimates or repeated runs are reported.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests validation loss across model sizes, but not loss scaling with dataset size or compute, nor whether the relationship is a power law over several orders of magnitude.
No small-run fit is used to predict the loss of larger runs.
No fixed-compute search for an optimal parameter/token allocation is reported.
The study does not compare depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The experiments concern text models and do not test other modalities or the listed training regimes as tests of the same power-law form.

The study reports selected zero-shot downstream-task results against model size and comments on pretraining loss as an indicator, but does not establish a general predictive mapping from pretraining loss to downstream performance.
The study does not compare fitting methods, parameter-counting choices, or alternative scaling-law fits.

rows.subject: chemistry models (S, M, L, XL; aggregate trend)
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation cross-entropy loss across model sizes.

conditions.value: validation cross-entropy loss in nats, averaged over a 2048-token context

rows.value: figure only; the text states that loss decreases as model size increases
rows.note: The authors say this confirms Kaplan et al., but provide no fitted exponent or numerical loss values in the text. The reported model-size range is less than one order of magnitude, so the result does not establish the claimed power-law form or its stated range.
rows.check: The direction (loss falls with size) is reported as observed, but only in Figure 2 with no numbers. The sweep spans about 8x in parameters, and the token budget is fixed (about 10B or 20B tokens), so larger models may be data-limited. The power-law form is not tested, so that part belongs under untested rather than a partial state.

rows.subject: chemistry models (S, M, L, XL; aggregate trend)
rows.operation_detail: Compared zero-shot downstream task performance across model sizes.
rows.value: The paper states performance increases with model size on SciQ, HT-CC, and ARC-E.
rows.note: This is the authors' aggregate statement across the named tasks; the tables give results for individual model/data combinations.
rows.check: The authors cite Table 5, but SciQ, HT-CC and ARC-E are in Table 4. Table 4 shows gains with size for AMiner, CORE, MAG and PubMed-F (e.g. CORE SciQ 0.69→0.78). S2ORC and WoS are flat on SciQ (0.31,0.31,0.31,0.30 and 0.37,0.34,0.37,0.39). The aggregate statement overstates consistency.

rows.subject: chemistry models (S, M, L, XL; aggregate trend)
rows.operation_detail: Compared zero-shot downstream task performance across model sizes.
rows.measure: Relationship between model size and downstream task performance
rows.value: The paper states there is no clear relationship between task performance and model size on the remaining benchmark datasets.
rows.note: The paper does not name all of the remaining datasets in this summary; their individual results appear in Tables 4–5.
rows.check: This is the authors' aggregate statement. Many of these tasks sit near chance for all models (e.g. WIC about 0.50, MathQA about 0.21), so floor effects may explain the absence.

rows.subject: XL (4x)
rows.operation_detail: Compared a model trained with a four-times-larger batch size against the similar-sized XL model.
rows.note: The paper describes XL (4x) as trained with a four-times-larger batch size and says it achieves the best SciQ performance.
rows.check: XL (4x) sees about 4x more tokens through a 4x larger batch at the same step count. Token count and batch size are confounded, and this is a single comparison with no uncertainty. It bears on data scale, not model size.

rows.subject: XL (4x)
rows.operation_detail: Compared a model trained with a four-times-larger batch size against the similar-sized XL model.
rows.note: Lower perplexity is better; the paper states XL (4x) achieves the lowest Lambada perplexity among its models trained from scratch.
rows.check: Same confound of tokens and batch size as R4. Lambada perplexity is a language-modelling measure on out-of-domain text, not a task accuracy.

rows.subject: XL (4x)
rows.operation_detail: Compared a model trained with a four-times-larger batch size against the similar-sized XL model.
rows.note: Lower perplexity is better; the paper states XL (4x) achieves the lowest WikiText perplexity among its models trained from scratch.
rows.check: Same confound of tokens and batch size as R4. WikiText perplexity is a language-modelling measure on out-of-domain text.

relationships.condition: Chemistry GPT-NeoX models, 0.18B–1.47B, fixed token budget
relationships.reason: Validation loss decreases monotonically with model size (Figure 2, figure-only). The power-law form is untested (R1).
relationships.display_finding: Validation loss decreased monotonically with model size, without a test of the power-law form.

relationships.condition: SciQ, HT-CC and ARC-E for AMiner, CORE, MAG and PubMed-F sweeps; more tokens for XL (4x) vs XL
relationships.reason: Accuracy rises with size on these tasks and corpora. XL (4x) beats XL on SciQ (0.84 vs 0.79), Lambada (30.40 vs 71.43) and WikiText (33.05 vs 48.65) (R2, R4–R6).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy increased with model size across the specified tasks and corpora; longer XL training improved SciQ from 0.79 to 0.84 and reduced Lambada from 71.43 to 30.40 and WikiText from 48.65 to 33.05.

relationships.condition: Remaining zero-shot benchmarks, and SciQ for S2ORC and WoS sweeps
relationships.reason: The authors report no clear size relationship on the other benchmarks. Table 4 shows flat SciQ for S2ORC and WoS, often near chance (R2, R3).
relationships.display_finding: Several zero-shot benchmarks show no clear size relationship, with SciQ performance flat and often near chance across S2ORC and WoS sweeps.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
